questions.stem: A sales-enablement lead finds that the team's Claude Project for drafting customer quotes has been giving last year's volume-discount tiers for about three weeks. The new rate card had been uploaded, but the old one was never removed. She has now deleted the old file and confirmed with known-answer questions that the project gives the right tiers. About 20 reps use the project. What is the MOST important next step?

options.text: Add a project instruction telling Claude to always prefer the newest rate card whenever two versions appear in the knowledge base.
Leave things as they are, since the configuration is now fixed and every future answer will use the correct discount tiers.
Tell the reps what was wrong and over which dates, and ask them to recheck quotes drafted with the project in that window.
Ask Claude to look back through the project's chats and list every quote that used the old tiers so the affected reps can be told.

questions.explanation: Fixing the configuration stops **new** wrong answers, but quotes drafted during those three weeks may already be with customers. The *inform* part of maintenance means telling the people who rely on the project **what changed, from when, and what to recheck**. Wrong pricing that reaches customers is a high-impact error, so a quiet fix is not enough.

whyWrong.A: The old file is already gone, so this rule fixes nothing today. It also does nothing about quotes that may already have gone out with the wrong tiers.
whyWrong.B: This is a silent fix. Reps who already sent quotes with the old tiers have no reason to recheck them, so the customer-facing errors stay in place.
whyWrong.D: This hands the impact check to the model instead of the people who sent the quotes. A generated list can miss or invent quotes, and reps stay uninformed while it is produced.

questions.mindset: A fixed configuration doesn't fix answers people already acted on. Tell them.

questions.stem: The owner of a customer-support drafting Project plans four improvements before the holiday rush: shorten the instructions, replace the returns policy with a new version, add a synced Google Doc of shipping cut-off dates, and remove two old FAQ files. She already has eight benchmark questions with known answers. If anything gets worse, she wants to know exactly which change caused it. Which plan is MOST effective?

options.text: Run the benchmark first to get a baseline, then make the changes in small steps and re-run the benchmark after each step.
Make all four changes in one sitting, then run the benchmark once and investigate any failing questions individually afterwards.
Make all four changes, then ask Claude in a new project chat to compare the new setup with the old one and flag any problems.
Set up a new project with the same instructions and knowledge, make all four changes there, and let the support team switch over once they like how it feels.

questions.explanation: Two things make a change attributable: a **baseline** taken before anything changes, and **one change at a time**, each followed by the same known-answer test. If question 5 breaks right after the instructions were shortened, she knows the cause at once. Bundling changes hides cause and effect, and known-answer testing against a fixed question set is exactly what evaluation guidance recommends for catching regressions.

whyWrong.B: With no baseline and four changes made together, a failing question could come from any of them. She would have to undo changes one by one to find the cause, which is the problem she wanted to avoid.
whyWrong.C: Claude cannot see the old configuration to compare against, and a self-review is not a known-answer test. This swaps the benchmark for the model's opinion of itself.
whyWrong.D: The new project still bundles all four changes, and 'they like how it feels' is not a test. Two parallel projects also mean two configurations to maintain.

questions.mindset: Baseline first, then change one thing at a time and re-test.

questions.stem: A legal operations team shares a 'Contract Clause Helper' Project with about 150 staff across the business. Many users don't realise it only covers the company's standard supplier contracts, and some have relied on it for employment-contract questions it was never built for. The owner also gets frequent messages asking whether its content is up to date. What is the BEST way to address both issues?

options.text: List every topic the project does not cover in its instructions so that Claude can refuse each of them one by one.
Limit access to the legal team only, so that people elsewhere in the business can no longer open or use the project.
Ask Claude to open every answer with a paragraph explaining what the project covers and when it was last reviewed.
Add a short 'About this project' note (purpose, sources, owner, last review date) and an instruction to flag out-of-scope questions.

questions.explanation: Both problems are **inform** problems: users don't know what the project is for, what it draws on, or how current it is. A short note people see when they open the project (for example in its description) answers those questions once. A standing instruction to say when a question falls outside supplier contracts, and to point to the right team, covers the cases the note doesn't prevent. The owner updates the review date at each review.

whyWrong.A: An ever-growing list of excluded topics is brittle and never complete. It also tells users nothing about sources or how current the content is.
whyWrong.B: The wider business is the intended audience. Removing their access throws away the project's value instead of explaining its scope.
whyWrong.C: This repeats the same paragraph in every answer, and the review date would have to be hard-coded into the instructions and kept up to date there as well.

questions.mindset: Tell users what a configuration is for, what it uses and how current it is. Don't leave them to guess.

questions.stem: A finance operations team shares a Project that answers staff questions about expense limits and approval routes. The expense policy changes roughly once a quarter. Last month two colleagues edited the instructions on the same day with conflicting changes, and nobody noticed that the knowledge base still held a superseded policy. Which TWO changes would BEST keep this project accurate over time? Choose TWO.

options.text: Give every member edit access so whoever spots a problem can fix it straight away without waiting for anyone else.
Name an owner and a backup who hold edit access, put everyone else on view access, and give them a clear way to report issues.
Have Claude end every answer with a reminder telling staff to double-check the figures against the official expense policy.
Re-upload every file in the knowledge base each Monday so that Claude always has a freshly loaded copy of each document.
Set a review tied to the quarterly policy cycle, in which the owner swaps documents, re-tests with known questions and logs changes.

questions.explanation: Both failures were **ownership** failures: too many editors, and nobody responsible for checking the sources. A named owner with edit rights (others on *can view*) stops conflicting edits. A review **timed to when the policy actually changes**, with re-testing and a change log, catches superseded files before staff do.

whyWrong.A: Broad edit access is what caused the conflicting changes last month. When everyone maintains a project, no one owns its accuracy.
whyWrong.C: A disclaimer shifts the work to every reader and leaves the superseded policy in place. Staff would still get wrong limits, just with a warning attached.
whyWrong.D: Re-uploading the same files changes nothing and doesn't remove the superseded policy. It is busywork that isn't tied to when the policy really changes.

questions.mindset: Accuracy needs an owner and a review cadence that matches how fast the content changes.

questions.stem: A product team's Project was set up to help employees write internal release notes. Its instructions name the audience as 'engineers and support staff' and allow internal ticket numbers and code names. Its knowledge base holds the internal roadmap, an export of known issues and the public style guide. Leadership now wants the project used to draft customer-facing release notes too. Which TWO updates are MOST necessary before customer drafts are produced? Choose TWO.

options.text: Rewrite the audience, tone and hard rules in the instructions for customers, including a rule against code names and ticket numbers.
Add a closing line to the instructions asking Claude to double-check every draft for anything that might sound confidential.
Upload a set of competitors' recent release notes so Claude can learn what public-facing release notes usually look like.
Take internal-only sources such as the roadmap and issues export out of the project, or run customer drafting in a separate project.
Switch to a larger model for customer drafts, because public communication needs a higher standard of writing quality.

questions.explanation: A change of **audience** is a maintenance trigger. Two layers are now wrong. The **instructions** still describe an internal audience and permit internal details. The **knowledge** still contains material customers must not see, which Claude may draw on. Fix both: rewrite the instructions for the new audience, and remove the internal sources (or keep the two uses in separate projects so each has the right knowledge). Removing the exposure is a control; asking the model to self-police is not.

whyWrong.B: Asking the model to police itself is not a control. The roadmap is still in the knowledge base and the instructions still allow internal detail, so leaks stay likely.
whyWrong.C: Competitors' notes don't reflect this company's voice or facts, and they do nothing about the internal audience or the confidential sources.
whyWrong.E: Writing quality isn't the problem. A larger model would still follow instructions aimed at engineers and could still quote the internal roadmap.

questions.mindset: When the audience changes, update both who the instructions address and what the knowledge exposes.

questions.stem: A company updates its AI usage policy: personal contact details of external people may no longer be stored in Claude Projects. A recruiting team's Project still contains a spreadsheet of candidate names and email addresses used to personalise outreach drafts, and its instructions say 'Use the candidate sheet to address each person by name.' Which TWO actions BEST bring the project into line with the new policy? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add an instruction telling Claude never to repeat any email addresses from the candidate sheet in the drafts it writes.
Keep the sheet but rename it clearly so everyone knows it contains personal data and must be handled with extra care.
Remove the candidate sheet from the project knowledge, replacing it with an anonymised version only if one is still needed.
Pause all use of the project until the next annual policy review, when the whole setup can be revisited properly.
Update the instructions so they no longer refer to the sheet, and tell the team how outreach drafting works from now on.

questions.explanation: A change in **organisational AI policy** is a maintenance trigger. The policy is about what is **stored**, so the data has to come out of the knowledge base — the same reasoning as removing or anonymising regulated identifiers before use. The instructions then point at a file that no longer exists, so they need updating too, and the team needs to be **told** the new way of working (for example, adding names when they send the message).

whyWrong.A: The contact details would still be stored in the project, which is what the policy forbids. An output rule doesn't change what is stored.
whyWrong.B: A clearer label doesn't make storing the data compliant. The policy says the data may not be there at all.
whyWrong.D: The fix is quick and clear now. Waiting months for a review stops useful work for no reason and leaves the non-compliant file in place in the meantime.

questions.mindset: A policy change about stored data is fixed by changing what is stored, then the instructions and the people.

questions.stem: A team's Project instructions say: 'Every Friday, compile the week's client updates from Gmail and send the summary to the account managers.' Their workspace Owner has just set the Gmail connector so that sending email is Blocked, while reading and drafting are still allowed. Since then, team members get confused or failed responses when they run the Friday task. What is the BEST update to the configuration?

options.text: Ask the Owner for an exception that switches sending back on just for this team so the original instructions keep working.
Change the instructions so Claude prepares the summary as a Gmail draft, and a team member reviews and sends it.
Remove the Gmail connector from the project and have team members paste each client update into the chat by hand.
Add a line telling Claude to retry the send step until it succeeds, then report back once the email has been delivered.

questions.explanation: When an Owner changes a connector's permissions, the **instructions have to match the new reality**. Blocking sends was a deliberate governance decision, and reading and drafting are still allowed. Rewriting the task as "draft, then a person sends" keeps nearly all the value, follows the control, and adds a human check before anything reaches the account managers.

whyWrong.A: This works against a deliberate organisation-level control instead of adapting to it. The configuration should follow governance, not the other way round.
whyWrong.C: Reading Gmail is still allowed. Dropping the connector throws away the useful part and brings back manual copy-paste.
whyWrong.D: A Blocked action won't succeed however often it is retried. The instructions would still ask for something the workspace forbids.

questions.mindset: When governance changes a connector, update the instructions to fit the control. Don't route around it.

questions.stem: The person who built and maintains a widely used onboarding Project is leaving the company in two weeks. She is the only person with edit access. What should happen before she leaves so the project stays maintainable?

options.text: Copy the instructions into a shared document so that anyone can rebuild the project from scratch if something goes wrong.
Switch the project to organisation-wide visibility so that everyone can see it and report any problems they happen to find.
Ask Claude to write a summary of how the project works and add that summary to the project's own knowledge base.
Give a named successor edit access and hand over the change log, the review schedule and the benchmark questions.

questions.explanation: Maintenance depends on an **owner** who can edit and who knows how the project is kept current. Handing over edit rights **together with** the change log, the review cadence and the test questions keeps the ownership continuous instead of starting from zero.

whyWrong.A: A backup copy doesn't create an owner. Nobody would be reviewing or updating the live project, and rebuilding only starts after something has already gone wrong.
whyWrong.B: Visibility controls who can see and use the project, not who can maintain it. More viewers reporting problems helps only if someone can fix them.
whyWrong.C: A file in the knowledge base becomes material Claude may draw on when answering new starters. It doesn't give anyone edit rights or responsibility.

questions.mindset: Every shared configuration needs a named owner, and ownership has to be handed over, not just left behind.

questions.stem: During a scheduled review of a sales-support Project, the new owner finds the instruction 'Never mention the Starter bundle in any answer.' Nobody on the current team knows why it was added, and the Starter bundle appears on today's public price list. What is the BEST way to handle it?

options.text: Find out why it was added, from the change log or the previous owner, before deciding to keep or remove it, and record the reason.
Delete it straight away, since the bundle is on the public price list and any rule nobody can explain is safe to drop.
Keep it unchanged indefinitely, because removing a rule that someone added on purpose could bring back an old problem.
Ask Claude inside the project why the rule exists, then keep or delete it depending on the explanation Claude gives.

questions.explanation: Instructions should be reviewed, but an unexplained rule may exist for a reason the price list doesn't show (a contract, a regional restriction, a pending withdrawal). The right move is to **find the reason** before changing anything, then **write it down** so the next reviewer doesn't face the same puzzle.

whyWrong.B: Being on the public price list doesn't prove the rule is obsolete. Deleting it without checking risks breaking an agreement or restriction nobody remembered.
whyWrong.C: Keeping every unexplained rule forever is how instructions bloat. This one may now contradict current sales guidance and cost the team valid answers.
whyWrong.D: Claude can't know why a person added the rule. It would produce a plausible-sounding guess, not the real reason.

questions.mindset: Know why a rule exists before you change it, and record the why for the next person.

questions.stem: A support team keeps a 'Known Issues' Google Doc that engineers update several times a week. Every Monday a coordinator downloads it as a PDF and re-uploads it to the team's Project, but she sometimes forgets, and Claude then suggests out-of-date workarounds. Which change BEST reduces this maintenance burden?

options.text: Add an instruction reminding Claude that the Known Issues file may be out of date and asking it to say so in every answer.
Upload the PDF twice a week instead of once, and keep the earlier copies so Claude can see how the issues have changed.
Add the Google Doc to the project from Google Drive, so the project stays in sync with the version the engineers edit.
Paste the full text of the Known Issues document into the project instructions so that it is always read first.

questions.explanation: An uploaded file is a **snapshot** that someone has to refresh by hand. Content added from Google Drive syncs with the live source, so Claude works from the latest version the engineers maintain. For content that changes several times a week, linking the live source removes the manual step that keeps failing.

whyWrong.A: A warning tells users the answer might be stale but doesn't make it current. It also puts a disclaimer on every answer, even correct ones.
whyWrong.B: This doubles the manual work and keeps superseded copies side by side, which leads to conflicting answers about which workaround applies.
whyWrong.D: This is still a manual copy that goes stale, it bloats the instructions, and it puts facts in the place meant for behaviour.

questions.mindset: Fast-changing content belongs in a synced source, not a hand-refreshed upload.

questions.stem: A customer-support team owns a Project that drafts replies using uploaded product manuals and the refund policy. The owner reviews it every quarter. Which TWO events should prompt the owner to review and re-test the project straight away, rather than waiting for the next scheduled review? Choose TWO.

options.text: A team member renames several chats in the project so they are easier to find in the sidebar later on.
The company publishes a revised refund policy that changes which purchases qualify for a full refund.
Use of the project rises by about a third after it is mentioned in the monthly team newsletter.
Several agents report that drafts recommend a troubleshooting step for a feature that has been removed.
A new agent joins the team and is given view access to the project as part of standard onboarding.

questions.explanation: A review schedule is a floor, not a ceiling. Some events should trigger an **immediate** update: a **source document changes** (the uploaded refund policy is now superseded), or **users report wrong or outdated answers** (the manuals no longer match the product). Either way, Claude will keep answering from the stale material just as confidently until someone updates it.

whyWrong.A: Renaming chats helps people find them but changes nothing Claude reads, so the project's instructions and knowledge are unaffected.
whyWrong.C: More usage isn't a sign of inaccuracy. It may raise the stakes, but nothing in the configuration has gone out of date.
whyWrong.E: Adding a viewer is routine access management. The knowledge, instructions and connectors stay exactly as they were.

questions.mindset: Source changes and user error reports are triggers to update now, not at the next review.

questions.stem: A retailer's customer-reply Project has this line in its instructions: 'Our return window is 30 days.' Last month the uploaded Returns Policy was replaced with a version that says 14 days. Since then, drafts sometimes quote 30 days and sometimes 14. The team wants answers that are correct now and stay correct the next time the policy changes, with the least ongoing upkeep. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Change the instruction line to say 14 days, so that the instructions and the uploaded policy now state the same figure.
Remove the figure from the instructions and tell Claude to take return terms from the current Returns Policy file.
Delete the Returns Policy file and rely on the instruction line, updating that one line whenever the window changes.
Add a rule telling Claude that whenever the instructions and the knowledge files disagree, the files always take priority.

questions.explanation: The same fact lives in **two places**, and only one was updated. The durable fix is **one source of truth**: the policy file holds the fact, and the instructions only say where to find it. The next policy change then needs one update, not two.

whyWrong.A: This fixes today's mismatch but keeps two copies of the fact. The next time the window changes, the same drift will happen again.
whyWrong.C: The instruction line can't carry the policy's detail (exceptions, conditions, excluded items), and instructions are meant for behaviour, not reference facts.
whyWrong.D: This works around the duplicate instead of removing it. The stale figure stays in the instructions, and every future conflict depends on a tie-break rule.

questions.mindset: Keep each fact in one place. Instructions point to knowledge, they don't copy it.

questions.stem: A project owner replaces an outdated pricing sheet in her Project's knowledge base with the corrected one and deletes the old file. To check the fix, she goes back to the long chat where she first noticed the wrong price and asks the same question again. Claude repeats the old price. What is the MOST likely explanation, and the best next step?

options.text: That chat already contains the earlier wrong answer, which can shape the reply. She should re-test in a new chat in the project.
Knowledge changes take several days to reach Claude. She should wait a week and then ask the question again in that chat.
Claude has permanently learned the old price. She should add an instruction to the project that states the correct price.
The new file must have failed to upload. She should upload it several more times until the correct price comes back.

questions.explanation: Everything earlier in a conversation stays in its context, **including the wrong answer** Claude gave before, and context shapes the reply. Re-asking in that same chat is a confounded test. Verifying a configuration change means using a **fresh chat** in the project, ideally with the standard benchmark questions, so the result reflects the new knowledge and not the old conversation.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in Claude's documentation describes a multi-day delay for project knowledge. Waiting also leaves the misleading chat history in place.
whyWrong.C: Claude doesn't permanently absorb a project file into the model. Hard-coding the price in the instructions creates a second copy of the fact to maintain.
whyWrong.D: Repeated uploads create duplicate files, the very problem she just fixed, and don't address the real cause, which is the old chat history.

questions.mindset: Verify configuration changes in a clean test, not in a chat that already holds the old answer.

questions.stem: An employee recently moved from the marketing team to the legal team. Since the move, Claude's responses in all of her chats, including those inside the legal team's Project, keep adding upbeat, promotional phrasing. The legal Project's instructions ask for neutral, precise language. What should she check FIRST?

options.text: Whether the legal Project needs a larger knowledge base of legal documents so Claude has more formal writing to imitate.
Whether the legal team should switch to a different Claude model that is better suited to formal legal drafting work.
Whether she should start every chat by reminding Claude that she now works in legal and wants neutral wording.
Whether her account-wide custom instructions still describe her old marketing role and promotional style, and update them.

questions.explanation: The symptom shows up in **all** her chats, which points to the layer that applies everywhere: her **account-wide custom instructions**. Personal settings go stale when a person's role changes, just as project settings do when the content changes. Updating them removes the conflict with the legal Project's instructions at its source.

whyWrong.A: The problem appears in every chat, not just answers that use legal documents. More knowledge files don't remove a conflicting standing preference.
whyWrong.B: Changing the model is a disguise. Any model will try to follow her account-wide preference for promotional writing.
whyWrong.C: A reminder in every chat is a workaround that has to be repeated forever, and the stale setting keeps pulling in the other direction.

questions.mindset: A problem in every chat points to the layer that applies to every chat.

questions.stem: A strategy team uses a Skill that packages their quarterly business review format: the section order, chart conventions and a slide template file. The company has now adopted a new review template with different sections. Team members have started typing the new section list into each chat, with mixed results. What is the BEST way to update the setup?

options.text: Keep the Skill as it is and add the new section list to every team member's account-wide instructions as well.
Turn off the Skill entirely and rely on each person describing the new format clearly at the start of every chat.
Update the Skill's instructions and template file to the new format, test it on a sample review, and tell the team.
Create a second Skill for the new format next to the old one, so Claude can pick whichever seems more suitable.

questions.explanation: A Skill is packaged know-how (instructions plus resources such as templates) that Claude loads when relevant. When the underlying standard changes, **the Skill is the thing to update**. Otherwise it keeps loading the old format and fights with whatever people type. Test the updated Skill, then tell the team so they stop using their workaround.

whyWrong.A: The old Skill would still load with the old sections, creating a conflict. Account-wide instructions would also push review rules into every unrelated chat.
whyWrong.B: This throws away the packaged template and goes back to per-chat descriptions, which is exactly what is producing mixed results.
whyWrong.D: Keeping old and new versions side by side is the 'append instead of replace' mistake. Claude may load either one, so outputs stay inconsistent.

questions.mindset: When the standard changes, update the packaged source. Don't stack workarounds on top of it.
